sentences.text: Tarchia was a large Asian ankylosaurid, with some estimates placing its length between 5.5 and 8.5 meters and its weight up to 3 or 4.5 tonnes.
This animal possessed a broad, low-slung body supported by short, strong legs and was covered in protective skin ossifications known as osteoderms.
Its skull measured approximately 40 centimeters in length and 45 centimeters in width.
A preserved skull bears distinct tooth marks from the tyrannosaurid Tarbosaurus, proving that this predator hunted the armored dinosaur.
Despite its size, this herbivore likely weighed as much as 4.5 tonnes.
The genus was established after a Polish-Mongolian expedition uncovered an ankylosaurid skull near Khulsan in 1970.
Teresa Maryańska formally named and described the type species Tarchia kielanae in 1977.
Living in dry desert environments, Tarchia was a herbivore that fed as a low-level bulk feeder using its broad, sub-rectangular muzzle.
In 2001, researchers noted wear facets on teeth that suggest tooth-to-tooth occlusion, though these findings likely do not apply to the holotype since no teeth are preserved there.
Evidence of bite marks indicates that Tarchia was likely preyed upon by Tarbosaurus.
The species belongs to the family Ankylosauridae and the subfamily Ankylosaurinae.
In 2021, a new species named T. tumanovae was described from a specimen found in the Nemegt Formation.
A cladogram of the Ankylosaurinae was published in 2015 by Arbour and Currie.
Tarchia lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically from 83.6 to 66 million years ago, spanning the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages.
Fossils were found in rocks representing eolian dunes, interdune environments, small intermittent lakes, and seasonal streams.

It is debated whether Dyoplosaurus giganteus is a valid species or a nomen dubium, leading some researchers to revive the name Tarchia kielanae. Furthermore, Arbour concluded that specimen PIN 3142/250, referred to Tarchia in 1977 by Tumanova, likely belonged to Saichania. This conclusion would radically change the common image of Tarchia, as this specimen had been the best preserved and the basis for most illustrations, museum mounts, and scientific research.
Researcher Arbour also concluded that Minotaurasaurus is a junior synonym of Tarchia based on shared distinguishing traits.
Vickaryous and colleagues in 2004 proposed that Tarchia was basal to two distinct clades of Late Cretaceous ankylosaurids.
